abstract: Crop improvement has long been constrained to genetic variations within cultivated germplasms and their wild relatives, which capture only a small fraction of historical protein diversity accumulated over evolutionary processes. Here, we propose the Beneficial Ancestral Genomic Sites concept, hypothesizing that restoring conserved ancestral acidic residues at phosphorylatable sites in plant proteins could substantially improve plant performance. We experimentally validate this concept with key immune-associated NADPH oxidases OsRbohB and OsRbohI to elevate broad-spectrum disease resistance in rice. Field-level testing of two competing models for growth-defense tradeoffs in plants strongly supports mitigating tradeoffs in modern agricultural settings. Our work unlocks a hidden, untapped reservoir of elite molecular variations inaccessible from conventional breeding resources, establishing a potentially transformative strategy for next-generation crop improvement under modern agriculture contexts.
